summary: The MCP subsystem is selfware's bridge to and from the Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio). As a client (McpClient over StdioTransport) it spawns third-party servers, performs the initialize handshake, discovers their tools via tools/list, and wraps each remote tool as an McpTool that plugs into the native ToolRegistry — extending the loop's action space with external capabilities. As a server (McpServer / run_mcp_server), selfware itself exposes its own tools and project resources to external agents. On the loop it is primarily an 'act' node: it enlarges what a ToolCall can reach and how Evidence flows in from outside the engine, while its handshake and capability negotiation touch 'perceive'.
context_basis: Recommendations were formed by reading src/mcp/ (client.rs, transport.rs, tool_bridge.rs, discovery.rs, server.rs, mod.rs) in the context of the full engine's ~600k-token budget framing, so each move accounts for how MCP tools compete for the same budget and ToolRegistry as native tools.

examples.title: Spawn a server and handshake before acting
examples.intent: Bring an external MCP server online so its tools become visible to the loop before any acting happens.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: McpClient::connect spawns the child via StdioTransport and runs initialize within init_timeout_secs; until the handshake returns serverInfo the server's tools do not exist on the canvas, so the planner cannot yet route ToolCalls to them.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Drag a server-config chip onto the canvas to instantiate a connection node; a spawn edge grows from it toward the loop's tool bus.
touch_interaction.visual: Node renders greyed with a spinning ring during the initialize handshake, then snaps to solid teal once serverInfo arrives.

examples.mini_scenario: The loop starts, connect() spawns the github MCP server, the handshake completes in 1.2s, and the node lights up ready to serve tools.
examples.pitfall: Do not let init_timeout_secs sit below 5s — connect() floors it at .max(5); a too-tight timeout kills a healthy but slow-booting server.

examples.title: Discover remote tools into the registry
examples.intent: Enumerate what the connected server can do and materialize each as an actionable node.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: discover_tools calls list_tools (tools/list) and wraps each schema in an McpTool with a name prefixed mcp_<server>_<tool>; these enter the ToolRegistry so the planner's action space grows without recompiling.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Spread two fingers over the connection node to fan its remote tools out as a cluster of child tool-nodes.
touch_interaction.visual: Each discovered tool blooms outward with a mcp_ badge; the count pill on the parent updates to the tool total.

examples.mini_scenario: After connecting, discover_tools returns 7 schemas; the canvas fans out mcp_github_create_issue, mcp_github_list_prs, and five more.
examples.pitfall: Names collide across servers if you drop the prefix — always keep mcp_<server>_ so two servers exposing 'search' stay distinct in the registry.

examples.title: Route a ToolCall to a remote server
examples.intent: Execute a step of the plan by invoking a tool that physically runs in another process.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: McpTool::execute forwards to McpClient::call_tool (tools/call); the loop's act step now spans a process boundary, so its latency and failure modes are governed by the transport, not local code.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap a remote tool-node to fire its execute; a pulse travels down the transport edge to the server process.
touch_interaction.visual: The edge animates a moving dot toward the external server glyph; the node flashes amber while in-flight.

examples.mini_scenario: The plan calls mcp_github_create_issue; the tap fires call_tool, the request crosses stdio, and the issue URL returns as Evidence.
examples.pitfall: Every call_tool holds a 60s transport timeout — don't wire a long-running remote op into a tight loop iteration without budgeting for that ceiling.

examples.title: Treat isError results as failures, not evidence
examples.intent: Prevent a tool-level error from being mistaken for a successful result and cached.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: call_tool inspects isError and stamps success:false so downstream success detection and the result cache never replay an error as a win; the verify step can branch to ErrorRecovery.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press a completed tool-node to reveal its raw MCP content and the derived success flag.
touch_interaction.visual: A red isError ribbon overlays the node when success is false, distinct from the green success ring.

examples.mini_scenario: mcp_db_query returns content with isError:true; call_tool flags success:false, so verify routes the loop into recovery instead of caching the payload.
examples.pitfall: Never cache on the presence of content alone — an isError result still carries a content array; gate caching on success:false.

examples.title: Negotiate framing without recompiling
examples.intent: Talk to a legacy server that speaks Content-Length headers instead of newline-delimited JSON-RPC.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: with_framing sets the outbound Framing per McpServerConfig; the read path auto-detects either framing, so a mismatched server no longer silently stalls the loop's perceive step.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Rotate the connection node to toggle its outbound framing between NewlineDelimited and ContentLength.
touch_interaction.visual: A small dial badge rotates between two glyphs; the send-edge restyles solid vs. dashed to reflect framing.

examples.mini_scenario: A legacy LSP-derived MCP server hangs on newline framing; rotating to ContentLength gets the handshake through.
examples.pitfall: Only override send framing — never force the read side; the auto-detector already handles servers that reply in the other framing.

examples.title: Match responses by request id
examples.intent: Keep concurrent in-flight requests from cross-wiring their responses.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: StdioTransport assigns a monotonic next_id per JsonRpcRequest and parks a oneshot in `pending`; the background reader routes each JsonRpcResponse by id, so parallel act nodes stay independent.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Pinch the transport node to collapse all in-flight requests into a single correlation lane showing id-to-response pairing.
touch_interaction.visual: Each pending id appears as a numbered token on the lane; tokens vanish as their responses land.

examples.mini_scenario: Two tools fire at once (id=4, id=5); the reader delivers each response to its own oneshot, so neither loop branch reads the other's result.
examples.pitfall: On write failure or timeout you must remove the pending id — a leaked slot accumulates one dead entry per failed request over the loop's lifetime.

examples.title: Sanitize the server's environment before spawn
examples.intent: Stop third-party server code from inheriting the operator's secrets.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: StdioTransport::spawn calls sanitize_command_env before applying the declared env, so the child never sees SELFWARE_API_KEY; the loop can safely delegate acts to untrusted code.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the spawn edge to inspect the sanitized env that will be handed to the child.
touch_interaction.visual: Inherited secrets render struck-through in red; only the declared env vars glow green as passed.

examples.mini_scenario: A community MCP server is spawned; sanitize_command_env clears the inherited AWS and API keys, and only the two env vars in its config reach it.
examples.pitfall: Do not re-export secrets via McpServerConfig.env as a shortcut — that defeats the firewall the sanitizer exists to enforce.

examples.title: Expose selfware's own tools as a server
examples.intent: Let an external agent drive selfware's ToolRegistry over MCP.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: run_mcp_server builds an McpServer wrapping the ToolRegistry and serves tools/list and tools/call over stdio; the loop's action space becomes the remote agent's, inverting client and host roles.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick the whole tool cluster outward past the canvas edge to publish it as a servable surface.
touch_interaction.visual: The cluster gains a broadcast halo and an inbound-arrow glyph indicating requests now flow in from outside.

examples.mini_scenario: Claude connects to `selfware mcp-server`, calls tools/list, and invokes file_read remotely; McpServer executes it against the local registry.
examples.pitfall: The registry is behind an RwLock — hold only a read lock for execute and take the write lock solely for activate(), or concurrent clients will contend.

examples.title: Gate all methods behind initialize
examples.intent: Refuse tool calls until the client has completed the handshake.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: McpServer::handle_request checks the `initialized` AtomicBool and rejects everything except initialize/ping/shutdown until it flips true, so no act runs on an unnegotiated session.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap the gate node to preview which methods are permitted in the current session state.
touch_interaction.visual: Locked methods show a padlock; they unlock with a green flash when the initialized flag flips.

examples.mini_scenario: A client calls tools/call before initialize; handle_request returns an INVALID_REQUEST-style refusal until the handshake lands.
examples.pitfall: Keep initialize/ping/shutdown outside the gate — locking those too would deadlock the handshake that opens the gate.

examples.title: Validate arguments against the tool schema
examples.intent: Reject malformed remote tool arguments before touching the registry.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: On tools/call McpServer runs validate_tool_arguments_schema and returns INVALID_PARAMS with the tool name and args in error.data, short-circuiting the act before ToolRegistry::execute.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the validation node to see the schema diffed against the incoming arguments.
touch_interaction.visual: Missing or mistyped fields highlight red in the schema overlay; a matching set glows green.

examples.mini_scenario: An external client omits a required 'path' field on file_read; validation returns INVALID_PARAMS and the tool never runs.
examples.pitfall: Return the JSON-RPC error code -32602, not a tool-level success:false — a schema violation is a protocol fault, not a tool outcome.

examples.title: Refuse destructive tools without explicit opt-in
examples.intent: Block destructive registry tools from being triggered remotely by default.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: McpServer checks Tool::is_destructive and refuses unless SELFWARE_MCP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=1, returning the refusal as a normal tool error so the remote loop can surface the reason and adapt.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Double-tap a destructive tool-node to toggle the ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE gate for the session.
touch_interaction.visual: Destructive nodes wear a red hazard stripe; enabling the flag swaps it for an unlocked-but-warned amber outline.

examples.mini_scenario: A remote agent calls shell rm; without the env flag McpServer returns a tool error explaining the block instead of deleting anything.
examples.pitfall: Return the block as a tool error (isError), not a protocol error — the client should read the reason, not just see a dead method.

examples.title: Activate deferred tools on first call
examples.intent: Make advertised-but-deferred tools callable the moment an external client asks for one.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: If a tool exists but isn't activated, McpServer takes a brief write lock, calls registry.activate, drops the lock, then executes — mirroring the agent's own discovery so every advertised tool is reachable.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap a dimmed (deferred) tool-node; it brightens as activation loads its schema, then fires.
touch_interaction.visual: Deferred nodes render translucent; a brief write-lock glyph appears, then the node solidifies and pulses.

examples.mini_scenario: A client calls an MCP resources tool for the first time; the server activates it under a short write lock, releases, and executes in the same request.
examples.pitfall: Release the write lock before execute — holding it across the tool run serializes all clients and stalls the server loop.

examples.title: Expose project resources over MCP
examples.intent: Let a remote agent perceive the project's files, structure, and config without local access.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: McpServer serves resources/list and resources/read for selfware://project/files, /structure, /file/<path>, and /config, feeding the remote loop's perceive step with grounded project state.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Spread over the server node to unfold its four resource URIs as a readable panel.
touch_interaction.visual: Each URI renders as a card; the config card carries a redaction shield glyph.

examples.mini_scenario: A remote agent reads selfware://project/structure to orient, then reads selfware://project/file/src/main.rs to plan an edit.
examples.pitfall: File reads canonicalize both path and root and enforce starts_with — never bypass that check or a symlink lets a client escape the project.

examples.title: Redact secrets from content-serving tools
examples.intent: Keep credentials out of results returned to an external client.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: After executing file_read, grep_search, or git_diff, McpServer runs redact_secrets on the content before framing the response, so no act leaks a key across the MCP boundary.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the response edge to preview the redacted-vs-raw content diff.
touch_interaction.visual: Redacted spans render as blurred bars; the edge carries a shield badge when redaction fired.

examples.mini_scenario: A remote grep_search hits a line containing an API key; redact_secrets masks it before the JsonRpcResponse leaves the server.
examples.pitfall: Apply redaction only to content-serving tools and config — running it blindly on structured tool output can corrupt legitimate payloads.

examples.title: Bound concurrency with a serving semaphore
examples.intent: Cap how many external requests run at once so the server can't be flooded.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: serve_io spawns handler tasks under a 32-permit semaphore and serializes output through a single writer, so inbound fanout stays within a fixed budget and frames never interleave.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Pinch the server node to reveal the permit meter and the queue of waiting requests.
touch_interaction.visual: A 32-slot gauge fills as permits are taken; overflow requests stack in a translucent queue below.

examples.mini_scenario: Forty requests arrive; 32 run immediately and 8 wait for permits, while the lone writer drains responses in frame order.
examples.pitfall: Don't let handler tasks write directly to stdout — bypassing the single writer lets two responses interleave and corrupt framing.

examples.title: Shut down a client cleanly
examples.intent: End a server connection without leaking the child process or reader task.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: shutdown sends a shutdown request then a notifications/exit, waits briefly, kills the child, and aborts the reader; the loop reclaims the process budget it borrowed for that server.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick the connection node off the canvas to trigger its graceful shutdown sequence.
touch_interaction.visual: Node plays a shrink-and-fade; a brief exit glyph confirms the child was reaped.

examples.mini_scenario: The task completes; shutdown() asks the server to exit, then start_kill guarantees the process is gone even if it ignored the request.
examples.pitfall: Drop also reaps via try_lock + start_kill — rely on that safety net, but still call shutdown() explicitly so the server gets its graceful exit chance.

examples.title: Send a fire-and-forget notification
examples.intent: Signal the server without occupying the request/response correlation table.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: notify writes a JSON-RPC message with no id (e.g. notifications/initialized), so it never parks a oneshot in `pending` — the loop advances without awaiting a reply.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick a small pulse from the client node toward the server to emit a one-way notification.
touch_interaction.visual: A thin dashed pulse travels the edge and dissipates with no return animation, marking no reply expected.

examples.mini_scenario: After initialize succeeds, the client fires notifications/initialized so the server knows the handshake is complete.
examples.pitfall: Never assign an id to a notification — a server that tries to respond to one produces an orphan response the reader can only log and drop.

examples.title: Drain stderr so the server can't deadlock
examples.intent: Prevent a chatty server from filling its stderr pipe and blocking.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: spawn takes the child's stderr and drains it on a background task into tracing; without this a full OS pipe buffer would stall the server and freeze every act routed through it.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Double-tap the transport node to open a live stderr tail from the drained server.
touch_interaction.visual: A scrolling log strip appears beneath the node; a warning tint shows if the drain task has exited.

examples.mini_scenario: A verbose server logs heavily on stderr; the drain task keeps the pipe empty so the JSON-RPC exchange on stdout never blocks.
examples.pitfall: Never leave stderr piped-but-unread — the buffer fills, the child blocks on write, and the whole loop hangs waiting for a response that can't come.

examples.title: Surface JSON-RPC errors as loop failures
examples.intent: Turn a protocol-level error into an explicit loop failure the planner can react to.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: When a JsonRpcResponse carries an error, request() bails with the JsonRpcError code and message; the act fails loudly rather than returning an empty result, letting verify branch to recovery.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press a failed edge to read the JSON-RPC error code and message inline.
touch_interaction.visual: The edge turns red and displays a [code] message chip; the node gains an error badge.

examples.mini_scenario: tools/list returns a -32603 internal error; request() bails, the tool-node shows the error, and the loop re-plans without that server.
examples.pitfall: A response with neither result nor error is still a fault — request() must error on a missing result, not hand back a silent null.

examples.title: Compose two servers into one action space
examples.intent: Blend tools from multiple MCP servers into a single planner-visible toolset.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: Each server's discover_tools contributes prefix-namespaced McpTools into the same ToolRegistry, so a single plan can chain mcp_github_* and mcp_db_* steps as if they were native.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Draw a connection from a github tool-node to a db tool-node to sequence a cross-server plan step.
touch_interaction.visual: The linking edge shows two distinct server-color segments meeting at a junction, marking the federation boundary.

examples.mini_scenario: A plan reads an issue via mcp_github_get_issue, then writes a row via mcp_db_insert — two servers, one loop iteration.
examples.pitfall: Federated tools share the engine's single budget and registry — a slow server's 60s timeout stalls the whole chain, so order fast tools first.
